measurement.happened:
This week in Iraq was dominated by three intertwined stories: the final assembly of a new government, a sharp economic shock, and a steady drumbeat of low-intensity security incidents.

The biggest political story was the completion of Prime Minister al-Zaidi's cabinet. On October 15, parliament approved the remaining ministerial posts and the deputy prime minister positions, effectively closing out the cabinet-formation process that had been dragging on. Al Jazeera's October 16 headline frames this as happening 'amid growing economic concerns,' which tells you the political class was under pressure to finish the job quickly rather than perfect it. The most eye-catching detail, picked up by both Reuters and the Associated Press, is that the new deputy prime minister is a figure already on the US sanctions list. That is not a small thing. It means the new government is seating a sanctioned individual in one of its two most powerful offices, which will almost certainly rattle Washington and the Iraqi opposition, and it signals that al-Zaidi's coalition is leaning heavily on a Shia or PMF-linked bloc that the US has been trying to pressure. The cabinet is now in place, but its internal balance and its relationship with Baghdad's foreign creditors and partners are now the open questions.

On the economic front, the headlines paint a picture of a country running out of breathing room. Al Jazeera reported on October 15 that Iraq devalued the dinar specifically to ease a cash crunch, leaving traders 'in limbo.' A devaluation of this kind is rarely a calm, planned decision; it usually means the central bank's foreign-currency reserves are thin, the parallel-market spread has become politically painful, and the government needed a fast lever to stop the dinar from sliding further on its own. Traders and importers, who had been pricing in the old rate, are now scrambling to reprice contracts, which will feed into a short-term inflation spike on imported goods. Two days later, on October 17, Bloomberg reported that Iraq is formally seeking an IMF program and that the Fund's chief has pledged 'firm' support. That pairing is telling: the government is signaling to markets and to its own population that it is not flying blind, while the IMF's public backing is a confidence signal aimed at creditors and at the dinar. The subtext is that Iraq's oil revenues are not covering its fiscal bill, and the government is looking for a multi-year fiscal adjustment framework. Expect the IMF mission to be in Baghdad within days.

Security stayed at the level of nuisance rather than crisis, but it was persistent. On October 14, a roadside bomb near Kirkuk killed an army brigadier and a soldier, which is a high-ranking enough loss to make the rounds in every military briefing but not large enough to trigger a change in posture. On October 17, an explosion at a base belonging to the Iraqi paramilitary alliance (the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF) killed one member. The PMF is a sprawling, multi-faction umbrella, and an explosion at one of its bases can be an accident, an internal dispute, or a targeted strike by a rival faction or by an external actor (Israel, the US, or a Turkish drone). With only one fatality and no immediate claim, it reads more like a low-level internal friction or a small munitions accident, but it keeps the PMF's internal politics in the news.

On the diplomatic front, Al Jazeera reported on October 14 that Iraq's prime minister told the Saudi crown prince that Iraqi territory would not be used for attacks. That is a strong public reassurance, and it almost certainly refers to the recurring pattern of Iran-aligned groups in Iraq launching missiles or drones toward Saudi or other Gulf targets using Iraqi airspace or launch sites. The PM's public commitment to Riyadh suggests either that a recent attack had put strain on the relationship, or that al-Zaidi is positioning himself as a reliable partner ahead of a possible Saudi-Iranian thaw or a new round of Gulf diplomacy. It is a small but meaningful signal that Baghdad wants to keep its equidistance credible.

A lighter note: Reuters reported on October 15 that bones found in an Iraqi cave are offering new clues about Neanderthal behavior, hinting at both violence and compassion. It is a small scientific story, but it adds to Iraq's long-running role as a cradle of early human history and gives the country a positive headline in a week otherwise dominated by politics and money.
measurement.expected:
Cabinet and politics. It is almost certain that the newly approved cabinet will hold its first full working sessions and begin the process of confirming budgets and appointments at the ministry level. The US-sanctioned deputy prime minister will be the focal point of foreign-policy friction: I would expect Washington to issue a statement within the next few days, either reaffirming that the sanctions stand or quietly opening a dialogue about a possible waiver. The Iraqi opposition, particularly the Sunni and Kurdish blocs, will use the sanctioned deputy PM as a talking point in parliament and in the media, so expect a few pointed speeches and possibly a no-confidence motion to be tabled, though I would not bet on it passing. Probability: almost certain for the first sessions; probable for a US diplomatic response; possible for an opposition motion.

Economy and the dinar. The devaluation will take full effect in the coming days, and I expect the parallel-market spread to narrow somewhat as banks adjust, but imported-goods prices will tick up. Traders who were 'in limbo' will reprice, and there may be a short window of hoarding or panic buying of staples, which could show up as a brief spike in retail prices. The IMF mission is probable to arrive in Baghdad within the next ten days, and the government will likely publish a brief statement of intent or a letter of intent by the end of the week. I would put the probability of a formal IMF program being signed this week at low, but the probability of substantive technical discussions starting is high. The government will also likely announce or hint at a fiscal consolidation package (spending cuts, tax adjustments, or a delay in salary payments to the public sector) to show the Fund it is serious. Probability: almost certain for market adjustment; probable for IMF mission arrival; possible for a fiscal announcement.

Security. The Kirkuk roadside bomb and the PMF base explosion are the kind of incidents that, in a calmer week, would be a footnote. But with a new cabinet in place and the PMF's internal politics still unsettled, I expect at least one more low-intensity security incident in the next seven days: another roadside IED in the Kirkuk-Anbar corridor, a small skirmish between PMF factions, or a drone or missile launch from Iraqi territory toward a Gulf or Israeli target. The PM's reassurance to Riyadh will be tested in practice. I would put the probability of at least one notable security incident at probable, and the probability of a larger coordinated attack (multiple missiles, a significant base strike) at possible but not the base case. The US and Israel will continue their low-profile monitoring and may carry out a small, deniable strike if a PMF faction misbehaves. Probability: probable for one incident; possible for a US/Israeli kinetic response.

Diplomacy. The Saudi-Iraqi channel is now warm, and I expect a follow-up call or a low-level working meeting within the week. The Kurdish region (KRG) will try to use the cabinet-formation moment to push for a resolution on oil-export transit fees and the status of the Erbil-Baghdad relationship, so a KRG delegation in Baghdad is probable. The US will maintain its steady-state pressure: sanctions reminders, a State Department readout, and possibly a quiet back-channel about the sanctioned deputy PM. Probability: probable for a KRG delegation; probable for a US diplomatic signal.

Public mood. The dinar devaluation and the cost-of-living squeeze will keep the middle class and the informal trading sector on edge. I would not expect a full-blown protest wave this week, but small, localized demonstrations in Baghdad, Basra, or the Anbar cities are possible, especially if salary payments to the public sector slip. The PMF's Shia base will be watching the cabinet composition closely and may organize a small rally or a social-media campaign if they feel their bloc was shortchanged. Probability: possible for localized protests; unlikely for a nationwide wave.

Less likely surprises. (1) A sudden resignation or public clash between al-Zaidi and the new deputy PM over a policy disagreement, which would be a dramatic scene but would require a very specific trigger. (2) A larger PMF base attack that kills more than a handful of fighters and forces Baghdad to publicly blame Iran or a rival faction, escalating the internal sectarian narrative. (3) The IMF mission arriving earlier than expected and issuing a preliminary assessment that is harsher than the government anticipated, creating a brief political crisis. (4) A surprise ceasefire or de-escalation signal from the Iran-aligned PMF that quiets the Gulf for a few weeks, which would be welcome but hard to sustain.

Things I would not bet on. A no-confidence vote actually passing against al-Zaidi this week, because the coalition that just assembled the cabinet is unlikely to turn on him within 48 hours. A full-blown civil-war-style escalation with the PMF splitting into two armed camps and fighting in the streets of Baghdad. A major natural disaster, a new pandemic, or a foreign invasion. A cabinet reshuffle or a new election being called. The dinar being re-pegged or the devaluation being reversed within the week. A landmark corruption trial or the arrest of a sitting minister.
emoji_reasons: The defining story of the week was parliament completing PM al-Zaidi's cabinet, including the politically charged appointment of a US-sanctioned deputy prime minister, which is pure government-and-parliament drama.

The dinar devaluation, the cash crunch, and the formal request for an IMF program put Iraq's fiscal and monetary crisis at the center of the week's news, making money and public finances the second dominant theme.

The roadside bomb that killed a brigadier near Kirkuk and the explosion at a PMF base that killed a member kept the drumbeat of armed violence and paramilitary instability in the headlines throughout the week.
